Senses.Explanation: A carpentry image for pulling out the nails and wedges that hold something fast. Two recensions explicitly pair it with loosening adhesions and removing bonds (解黏去縛), then reverse the image: “Here, for people, I add nails and set wedges, add rope and add bindings.” Elsewhere the phrase describes what buddhas do in appearing in the world, and Yuanwu Keqin uses it alongside releasing adhesions and bonds.

Senses.Explanation: The omitted-look procedure names the deletion of 顧, “look,” from the sequence 顧、鑒、咦. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1997.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuanwu Foguo. The phrase compares people of like feather, but the passages distinguish genuine affinity from a merely similar exterior. Sending out fundraisers, Yuanwu Keqin says a single tree makes no forest, one thread no cord, and no great building or river crossing depends on one timber or oar. Inside and outside, guest and host must answer one another, their kind and feathers matching. His following verse makes the monastery's work depend on the monks' shared service. The comparison supports cooperation in a concrete communal task, not a biological classification of practitioners.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J29/J29nB223.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shanhui. After a monk's answers and bow receive a blow, Shanhui Huan recalls a beckoning across a river followed by someone immediately going away, calling that shared taste and like feathers that save effort. He then contrasts his own assembly's dozing and dreamlike dullness: if he does not appear they suspect he withholds teaching, and if he does they resent pressure. Asked how to clear this suspicion and resentment, he pauses and says that if they have no contriving mind, he too will stop. The phrase praises responsive affinity, but the address uses that praise to expose present misunderstanding rather than congratulate all who belong to the group.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB388.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yikui of Shending. Taking his room, Yikui Yuankui says this is the place that tempers ordinary and sacred and catches phoenixes and dragons, so it needs genuine creatures of that kind. If the feathers only look similar and the horns merely approximate, he strikes his staff and compares it to a counterfeit rooster's voice deceiving people. He will not let it pass in confusion. Here the phrase marks superficial likeness under examination, in contrast to the cooperative or recognized affinity of other uses.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (L/L155/L155n1643.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Hongjue Min. At Tiantong's request to send a monk to sweep an ancestral stupa, Muchen Daomin recalls his late teacher Miyun's demanding work restoring the lineage and removing tangled views. He asks whether anyone of like feather and shared taste is present who can bear responsibility for the time and continue that ancestral conduct, then tells the messenger to encourage Elder Huishan. The likeness sought is a capacity to carry the work onward, rather than possession of a few matching formulas or a literal resemblance to the teacher's appearance.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: 大慧普覺禪師語錄: Yongjia Xuanjue utters the complete headword-bearing quoted line; Dahui Zonggao is the active outer raiser.

Senses.Explanation: “Reckless and unrestrained, one invites disaster” preserves the complete warning in 莽莽蕩蕩招殃禍: the heedless manner and its consequence belong together. Dahui Zonggao quotes Yongjia Xuanjue's line and directly applies it to a man's dismissal of action and consequence. The warning does not make 莽莽蕩蕩 a realization state; it condemns indiscriminate freedom that brushes consequences aside.

Senses.Note: Two independent Tier-2 families of related occurrences support this sense; lamp and lineage-compilation copies are excluded.

Senses.Explanation: The paired reduplication describes handling something roughly and without discrimination. Shixi Xinyue contrasts 莽莽鹵鹵 release with careful diagnosis and preparation. Nanyue Jiqi quotes Zhimen Guangzuo’s song using it for conduct as numerous as river sands. Xiaotang calls the two monks confused in his own response to the wind-and-banner case. Yian calls later practitioners muddled for pinning an extra peg into emptiness in his own brief talk.
